title: DfE Decoded 165 The EYFS Space Rules Are Staying For Now
author: Paul Urry
summary: Paul Urry unpacks the government's decision not to relax the Early Years Foundation Stage space requirements, after a consultation on letting outdoor free-flow space count toward indoor capacity. He notes the minimum indoor space figures remain unchanged for group and school-based providers, so there is no immediate operational change. The proposal tried to address a real expansion barrier, since many providers with waiting lists cite physical capacity. The uncapped option was overwhelmingly rejected, while the capped option split the sector 55 to 45, and schools were more cautious than other providers. Urry explains why the government stepped back: overcrowding when outdoor areas cannot be used, unclear definitions of free-flow, staffing and ratio pressures, and worries that denser, noisier rooms would harm children with SEND. His point for early years leaders is that capacity is not simply a floor-space calculation.
points: The minimum indoor space requirements per child are unchanged, so schools and nurseries cannot expand numbers by counting outdoor space.
The consultation split on the capped option, with 55 percent support overall but 54 percent of school respondents opposed and 70 percent of school-based respondents wanting the existing rules kept.
Overcrowding when weather, meals, naps or group activities force children inside was the strongest concern behind the decision.
Free-flow outdoor provision raises hard operational questions about definitions, supervision, ratios, shelter and toileting that make it harder to implement than it sounds.
Concern about burnout and about denser, more overstimulating rooms for children with SEND weighed heavily in the equality responses.
quotes: The government had been looking for a way to make it easier for early years providers to create more places. The proposal was to allow some outdoor free-flow space to count towards the existing indoor space requirements.
Nearly two-thirds of those commenting on equality impacts expressed concern that denser, noisier or more overstimulating environments could have a particularly negative effect on children with SEND.
But buildings do not suddenly become bigger because entitlement expands. That is the tension sitting underneath this entire consultation.
Schools appear to have been more cautious about relaxing the rules than some other parts of the early years sector.
A setting might technically have enough combined indoor and outdoor space to increase numbers. But if all those children then need to be indoors at the same time, the room becomes crowded.
There was a real concern that increasing capacity without increasing staffing capacity could worsen quality.
